reasoning: Operating billing and calculating machines produces calculations and billing documents that others use, so NO_DELIVERABLE (Y) misreads the category, which is for work that produces nothing anyone relies on. X codes the output at the level of the processing job and notes that it may largely duplicate the specific billing statements, which a reviewer should check.

For a billing clerk, monitoring equipment is incidental watching while machines run; the only items it produces, problems fixed or reported to repair staff, are exactly what 23249 covers. Y's NO_DELIVERABLE with an overlap to 23249 avoids counting the same flagged fault twice, which X's coding would do.

Clearing a jam is hands-on work, while reporting a major fault to repair personnel produces a repair request that someone acts on. These are different activities, and X splits them; Y codes the reporting as PHYSICAL too.

Both codings correctly split live and written inquiries. Y's larger live share fits billing clerks, whose rate and procedure questions mostly come by phone or at the counter, and Y's overlap lists are more complete.

A shipping label is a quick item for shipping staff, while a billing document or credit memo is a longer accounting document checked by billing or receivables staff. The statement covers very different kinds of item, so Y's split is better than X's vague mixed batch.

Answering phones, scheduling appointments and ordering supplies are different activities, and scheduling happens both live and from written requests. X applies both splits, while Y merges scheduling and ordering into one written item.

Returning or retrieving a check is physical handling, adjusting the account is back-office entry, and error inquiries come both live and in writing. Y separates all of these as the instructions require; X folds the physical handling into a DISCRETE item and treats all inquiries as live.
